glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Solomon tests pleasure, achievement, and wisdom and finds that none of them can overcome death or secure lasting gain, until at the chapter’s close he recognizes that the simple enjoyment of food, drink, and work comes “from the hand of God.”

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Ecclesiastes 2 continues the royal search Solomon began in 1:12, after his test of wisdom ended in grief (1:18). The chapter completes that search before a new poem about God’s times opens chapter 3.

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “Nothing is better for a man than that he should eat and drink, and that his soul should enjoy good in his labor. This also, I saw, was from the hand of God.” (Ecclesiastes 2:24)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Ecclesiastes 2 records what happened when a king who could try anything actually did. Solomon gave himself first to pleasure and then to building and gathering on a scale no one in Jerusalem had matched. One small word keeps coming back: he built himself houses, planted himself vineyards, made himself gardens and pools, and gathered for himself silver and gold (verses 4–8). Solomon was trying to build a satisfying life with his own hands, and as far as it went, the attempt worked. He admits that “my heart rejoiced in all my labor” (verse 10). Yet when he looked over the whole undertaking, his verdict was plain: “There was no profit under the sun” (verse 11).

In the end, wisdom fared no better. Solomon insists that wisdom excels folly “As light excels darkness” (verse 13), but the wise man dies like the fool and is forgotten just as quickly. Death also does more than end the worker. It hands everything he built to “the man who will come after me” (verse 18), who may turn out to be a fool. Solomon does not soften what this did to him. “Therefore I hated life,” he writes (verse 17), and he describes a worker whose heart “takes no rest” even at night (verse 23). These lines honestly report the low point of his search. They are not the book’s counsel for living.

Then the chapter turns. The same eating, drinking, and work that could not carry the weight of a self-made life are now received “from the hand of God” (verse 24). God is not named anywhere in verses 1–23, and it fits the whole search that He first appears at this turning point, where joy is received as a gift. Verse 26 places that joy within a relationship with Him, for God gives “wisdom and knowledge and joy to a man who is good in His sight.” The good things Solomon tried to seize for himself are given freely by a generous God.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Ecclesiastes 2:1–3 — Laughter and Wine Put to the Test

Having found that wisdom only brought grief, Solomon tells his heart, “I will test you with mirth,” and gives the verdict before he describes the experiment: “this also was vanity.” He calls laughter “Madness!” because, made the goal of life, it cannot produce lasting gain, and he tries wine while still “guiding my heart with wisdom,” searching for what is good for people to do “all the days of their lives.”

Ecclesiastes 2:4–11 — Great Works, Great Wealth, and No Profit

Solomon builds, plants, and gathers on a greater scale than anyone in Jerusalem before him, denies himself nothing his eyes desire, and genuinely enjoys the work. When he looks back over all of it, he concludes that it was “vanity and grasping for the wind” and that “There was no profit under the sun,” meaning that nothing lasting remained beyond the pleasure he had already received along the way.

Ecclesiastes 2:12–17 — Wisdom Excels Folly, Yet Both Die

Solomon weighs wisdom against folly and affirms that wisdom truly is better, as light is better than darkness. Yet “the same event happens to them all”: the wise man dies and is forgotten just like the fool, and that shared end brings Solomon to the words “Therefore I hated life.”

Ecclesiastes 2:18–23 — Labor Left to an Unknown Successor

Solomon hates his labor because he must leave it to a successor who may be wise or a fool, yet who will rule over everything he built. He then widens his own case into a general one: a person may work with wisdom, knowledge, and skill and still have to leave what he has gained to someone who never worked for it, while such toil brings sorrowful days and sleepless nights.

Ecclesiastes 2:24–26 — Enjoyment Received from the Hand of God

The chapter turns as Solomon sees that eating, drinking, and enjoying good in one’s labor come “from the hand of God,” a conclusion his own unmatched experience supports (verse 25). God gives wisdom, knowledge, and joy to the person who is good in His sight, while the sinner gathers for someone else, and the closing refrain most likely describes the futility of that gathering without cancelling the gift affirmed in verse 24.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
The verdict in this chapter comes from a witness who cannot easily be dismissed. Solomon had the wealth, the wisdom, and the freedom to try everything, and he found real pleasure along the way. When he reports that his achievements still left “no profit” (verse 11), he answers the book’s opening question about labor (1:3) with the weight of experience.

Scripture also lets grief over death and lost work be spoken aloud here. Ecclesiastes 2 does not name Christ, but read alongside 1 Corinthians 15, the problem it raises finds its answer in Him. Because Christ has risen as the firstfruits of the resurrection, labor in the Lord is not in vain. Work done in Him is neither erased by death nor lost to an unknown heir.

Finally, the chapter shows God as a generous giver. The enjoyment Solomon could not manufacture is received from God’s hand within a right relationship with Him. Pleasure failed as the foundation of life, but Scripture never forbids it, and received as God’s gift, it can be enjoyed with gratitude.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Pleasure and achievement put to the test. Solomon withholds nothing from himself and enjoys his work, yet the whole undertaking leaves no lasting gain (verses 1–11).

Wisdom’s real advantage and its limit. Wisdom excels folly as light excels darkness, but it cannot stop death or keep the wise from being forgotten (verses 13–16).

Labor that must be left behind. Death hands a worker’s achievements to a successor, and the worker cannot ensure that the heir will be wise or control what becomes of the work. Anxious toil cannot secure the gain it strives for (verses 18–23).

Enjoyment received from God’s hand. The simple pleasures that failed as a self-made foundation return as gifts God gives within a relationship with Him (verses 24–26).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
“Vanity.” The NKJV uses this word to translate a Hebrew word that pictures a breath or vapor, something that cannot be held. Solomon uses it to call life meaningless when it is pursued without God. In this chapter he applies it to pleasure, wisdom, and labor alike (verses 1, 15, 19, 26).

“Grasping for the wind.” This phrase pictures trying to hold what cannot be held. It pairs with “vanity” to describe effort that leaves nothing in the hand (verses 11, 17, 26).

“Under the sun.” The phrase marks Solomon’s examination of life inside earthly limits. He measures life by what people can see and achieve before the grave, and he leaves God’s revelation and future judgment out of the calculation. That limited view explains why his verdicts on labor sound so bleak (verses 11, 17–20, 22).

“Profit.” Profit is the lasting gain left after all of one’s labor, the very thing the book’s opening question asks about (1:3). Verse 11 answers that there was none, and verse 22 asks the same question again in personal terms.

“The same event.” This expression refers to death, which comes to the wise and the fool alike (verse 14). Death gives them the same earthly end, but it does not make them equal in character or in their standing before God.

“From the hand of God.” The enjoyment of food, drink, and work is received as God’s gift (verse 24). Solomon had already enjoyed his labor (verse 10), yet his achievements could not secure lasting satisfaction. Here enjoyment is something received from God’s hand, not a lasting gain won through achievement. This is the first of the book’s passages that commend joy as His gift.

focus: Ecclesiastes 2 carries Solomon’s royal search through to its verdict as he tests pleasure, then great works and wealth, weighs wisdom against folly in the face of death, and grieves over leaving his labor to an unknown successor. The chapter closes with Solomon recognizing that food, drink, and enjoyment in work come “from the hand of God” (verse 24).

sections.title: Laughter and Wine Put to the Test
Great Works, Great Wealth, and No Profit
Wisdom Excels Folly, Yet Both Die
Labor Left to an Unknown Successor
Enjoyment Received from the Hand of God

1.brief: Having found that wisdom only increased his grief (1:18), Solomon turns to pleasure as his next test, telling his own heart to “enjoy pleasure.” Before he describes the experiment, he gives its verdict: “this also was vanity,” meaning that pleasure, too, proved meaningless as a source of lasting satisfaction.
1.explain:
I said in my heart: Solomon reports a conversation with himself. In Scripture the heart is a person’s inner self, the place where thinking, desire, and decision meet. He has just ended his test of wisdom with the admission that “in much wisdom is much grief” (1:18). Now he turns to his own inner life and sets out the next step of his search.

Come now, I will test you with mirth: The word “test” shows that this is a deliberate experiment, not a slide into indulgence. Mirth is gladness and merriment, the lighthearted joy people feel at a feast or among friends. Solomon makes his own heart the subject of the trial. He will fill it with gladness and watch what happens.

therefore enjoy pleasure: Solomon gives himself permission, even a command, to take in pleasure fully. Nothing in the verse treats enjoyment as sinful. Verse 10 confirms that the pleasure he found was real: “my heart rejoiced in all my labor.” The question he is testing is whether pleasure can carry the weight of a life’s meaning.

but surely, this also was vanity: Before he describes the experiment, Solomon announces how it turned out. The NKJV word “vanity” translates a Hebrew word that pictures a breath or vapor, something that cannot be held. Solomon uses it to call pleasure meaningless as a source of lasting satisfaction. The word “also” places pleasure beside wisdom, the pursuit he has just tested and found wanting. His verdict concerns what pleasure can finally gain when it is made the foundation of life. It does not deny that he enjoyed it.
1.notes:
Solomon’s words “I said in my heart” continue a pattern from the opening of his search. In 1:16 he writes, “I communed with my heart,” and in 2:15 he uses the same form again: “So I said in my heart.” Solomon reports each stage of the experiment as a conversation with himself, so the reader hears both his plans and his conclusions.

The short phrase “this also” links the verdict on pleasure to the earlier verdict on wisdom: “I perceived that this also is grasping for the wind” (1:17). The same words mark each new verdict later in the chapter (verses 15, 19, 21, 23, 26). In verse 24, however, they introduce something different: “This also, I saw, was from the hand of God.”

2.brief: Solomon calls laughter “Madness!” and asks of mirth, “What does it accomplish?” He is weighing what laughter achieves when it is made the goal of life, and he finds that it cannot produce the lasting gain he is seeking. He is not condemning laughter itself as sinful.
2.explain:
I said of laughter—“Madness!”: Solomon’s one-word verdict is sharp. Laughter is good in its place, and the book itself later speaks of “a time to laugh” (3:4). But when laughter is made the goal of life, Solomon judges it senseless. It gives a moment of relief and then is gone, leaving nothing lasting behind. By calling it madness, he means that laughter cannot answer the question of what makes a life worthwhile.

and of mirth, “What does it accomplish?”: This question asks for a result. The book opened by asking, “What profit has a man from all his labor” (1:3), and Solomon now asks the same kind of question about gladness. He expects the answer that mirth, however pleasant, produces no lasting gain. He is measuring what laughter achieves, not passing moral judgment on laughter itself.
2.notes:
The word “Madness!” comes from the vocabulary of Solomon’s search. He had set his heart “to know wisdom and to know madness and folly” (1:17), and in verse 12 he turns “to consider wisdom and madness and folly.” His verdict therefore puts laughter, when it is made life’s goal, on the side opposite wisdom.

The NLT translates the verse, “Laughter is silly. What good does it do to seek pleasure?” “Silly” is much milder than the NKJV’s “Madness!”, and the NLT’s second question speaks of seeking pleasure instead of mirth. The NKJV keeps the sharper verdict and its verbal link to 1:17 and 2:12.

3.brief: Solomon next tries wine and deliberately takes hold of “folly,” yet he keeps “guiding my heart with wisdom,” so wisdom continues to direct his investigation even while he tests wine and folly. His aim is to discover “what was good for the sons of men to do under heaven all the days of their lives,” the question his whole search is trying to answer.
3.explain:
I searched in my heart how to gratify my flesh with wine: This test is also deliberate. Solomon planned how to use wine to please his “flesh,” meaning his body with its appetites and senses. Wine was a familiar source of cheer, and Solomon himself observes elsewhere that “wine makes merry” (10:19). Here wine becomes one more way to test whether pleasure can satisfy.

while guiding my heart with wisdom: This phrase keeps the experiment from turning into drunken abandon. Even while he tested wine, Solomon kept wisdom in charge of his inner life so that he could observe and judge what he experienced. Verse 9 makes the same point about the larger experiment: “Also my wisdom remained with me.” His verdict comes from a clear-minded observer, not from someone lost in excess.

and how to lay hold on folly: Solomon deliberately took hold of what he knew to be foolish. Folly is the opposite of wisdom, a way of living that sets sound judgment aside. He grasped it on purpose to examine it from the inside, so that his conclusion would come from experience and not from a safe distance.

till I might see what was good for the sons of men to do: Here Solomon states the purpose of the experiment. He wanted to discover what is truly good for people to do with their lives. Ecclesiastes uses “the sons of men” for human beings in general (2:8; 3:10), so the question concerns everyone, not only a king. It is the practical question behind the whole search: how should a person spend his life?

under heaven all the days of their lives: “Under heaven” sets the question in earthly life, the world people can see and touch. “All the days of their lives” reminds the reader that each person has only a limited number of days, and Solomon wants to know how those days are best spent. The chapter gives its first real answer in verse 24, where Solomon finds that enjoyment received “from the hand of God” is better than anything he could produce for himself.
3.notes:
The NLT words the purpose of the experiment differently: “I tried to experience the only happiness most people find during their brief life in this world.” The NKJV presents the aim as a question to be answered, “what was good for the sons of men to do.” In the NKJV, the experiment is a search for the right way to live. In the NLT, Solomon is sampling the pleasures ordinary people pursue. Both translations set the experiment within the limited span of human life.

Verse 3 uses “under heaven,” as 1:13 and 3:1 also do, while the rest of chapter 2 uses “under the sun” (verses 11, 17–20, 22). Both expressions refer to life on earth. The text does not explain why “under heaven” appears in this verse.

Solomon’s question about what is good for people to do returns in similar wording in 6:12: “who knows what is good for man in life, all the days of his vain life.” This repetition shows that the question reaches beyond the pleasure experiment and runs through the book.

4.brief: The test moves from pleasure to achievement as Solomon says, “I made my works great.” Houses and vineyards begin a long list of projects, and the repeated “myself” shows that he built and planted for his own satisfaction.
4.explain:
I made my works great announces a new stage in Solomon’s search. In verses 1–3 he tested laughter and wine; now he turns to accomplishment. The word “works” is broad enough to cover everything that follows, from buildings and gardens to servants and treasure. The phrase describes a deliberate program of achievement on a scale only a king could attempt, and the flow of the passage shows him undertaking it to see whether accomplishment could supply what laughter and wine did not.

I built myself houses, and planted myself vineyards names the first two projects. Houses and vineyards are the ordinary goods of a settled life, a place to live and a supply of fruit and wine. Solomon speaks of them in the plural, and the list that follows shows a scale far beyond ordinary need. The small word “myself” appears twice in this one verse, because Solomon was both the builder and the one meant to benefit. The experiment tests whether a man can make his own life satisfying through what he builds for himself.
4.notes:
In the NKJV, “myself” or “for myself” appears five times in verses 4–8: “built myself houses,” “planted myself vineyards,” “made myself gardens,” “made myself water pools,” and “gathered for myself silver and gold.” The repetition runs through the whole inventory and keeps Solomon at the center of every undertaking.

The NLT begins this verse with “I also tried to find meaning,” words that do not appear in the NKJV. The NLT states openly a purpose that the NKJV leaves to the flow of the passage, where Solomon is searching for “what was good for the sons of men to do” (verse 3).

5.brief: Solomon adds gardens and orchards planted with “all kinds of fruit trees,” places of beauty and delight that only great wealth could create. Like the houses and vineyards, he made them for himself, so they add abundance and pleasure to his experiment.
5.explain:
I made myself gardens and orchards moves from necessities toward beauty and delight. A house gives shelter and a vineyard produces a crop, but gardens and orchards are places to walk, rest, and enjoy. Creating them took land, workers, and money in abundance, and once again Solomon made them “myself,” for his own enjoyment.

and I planted all kinds of fruit trees in them stresses variety. Solomon did not settle for a few familiar trees; he gathered “all kinds.” Fruit trees take years to reach their full yield, so this was patient, long-range investment rather than a passing indulgence. The detail adds both abundance and pleasure to the experiment, and it prepares for the next verse, where those trees need water.

6.brief: To keep his groves growing, Solomon built “water pools,” an undertaking that required planning and labor on a large scale. The detail shows the reach of his work: he did more than plant, because he also built what was needed to keep his plantings alive.
6.explain:
I made myself water pools shows how far Solomon’s work extended. Planting trees is one task; keeping a large planting alive is another. Pools that could water whole groves required planning, construction, and continuing labor. The “myself” of the earlier verses appears again, because these pools also served Solomon’s own designs.

from which to water the growing trees of the grove explains why the pools were built. They existed to sustain the trees he had planted in verse 5, so one work supported another. Solomon’s achievement was a connected whole, carried through with resources, skill, and follow-through. Whatever verdict he reaches in verse 11 therefore cannot be blamed on a half-hearted attempt.

7.brief: Solomon’s possessions include people and livestock: male and female servants, servants born in his household, and herds and flocks greater “than all who were in Jerusalem before me.” The comparison shows that no one before him had been better placed to test whether abundance can satisfy.
7.explain:
I acquired male and female servants moves the inventory from land and buildings to people. A household of this size needed many hands to run it, and Solomon lists these servants among the possessions that made up his greatness.

and had servants born in my house adds a further mark of size and permanence. Besides the servants he acquired, his household included servants born within it, so the royal establishment was large and settled enough to grow from within.

Yes, I had greater possessions of herds and flocks adds livestock, another visible measure of wealth. The opening “Yes” presses the point home: his herds and flocks really were greater than anyone else’s.

than all who were in Jerusalem before me supplies the standard of comparison. Solomon measures himself against everyone who had lived in Jerusalem before him and finds no equal. The claim matters for the argument because it establishes that no earlier resident of Jerusalem was better placed to test abundance. If great possessions could make a life meaningful, they should have done so for him.
7.notes:
The NLT translates the comparison as “more than any of the kings who had lived in Jerusalem before me,” which limits it to earlier kings. The NKJV’s “all who were in Jerusalem before me” is broader and does not mention kings.

Where the NKJV says Solomon “acquired male and female servants,” the NLT reads “I bought slaves, both men and women.” Both translations list these people among the possessions of Solomon’s household.

8.brief: Solomon gathers royal wealth, “silver and gold and the special treasures of kings and of the provinces,” and he surrounds himself with singers and what the NKJV renders “musical instruments of all kinds.” By naming “the delights of the sons of men,” he shows that his search reached for the pleasures people prize most.
8.explain:
I also gathered for myself silver and gold turns to precious metals, the most direct measure of wealth. The words “for myself” continue the pattern of the earlier verses, because this treasure was also collected for Solomon’s own enjoyment.

and the special treasures of kings and of the provinces raises the scale again. The wording points to treasure of the kind that belongs to kings and comes from the provinces, the regions within a ruler’s domain. Ordinary wealth could buy houses and herds, but only a king could assemble a collection like this.

I acquired male and female singers moves from possessions to experience. Singers filled the court with music, and with them the inventory returns to the kind of pleasure Solomon began testing in verse 1.

the delights of the sons of men sums up what these acquisitions represent. “The sons of men” means human beings in general. Solomon used the same expression in verse 3 when he set out to discover “what was good for the sons of men to do.” By gathering the delights people everywhere value most, he made his test cover what humanity in general values.

and musical instruments of all kinds completes the list as the NKJV renders it. The Hebrew expression behind these words is uncertain, and translations differ widely in how they understand it. Whatever it names, the clause finishes a picture of extraordinary royal resources and unrestricted pursuit of delight. The argument of the chapter rests on that abundance, not on this one expression.
8.notes:
The Hebrew words translated “musical instruments of all kinds” are uncertain in meaning. The NKJV understands them as instruments, while other translations understand women or concubines; the NLT, for example, reads “had many beautiful concubines.” Some older renderings understand drinking vessels instead. Whichever meaning is correct, the verse describes extraordinary royal resources and pleasures.

Solomon’s many wives and concubines are recorded independently in 1 Kings 11:1–8. What Scripture says about his marriages therefore does not depend on how this uncertain phrase is translated.

9.brief: Solomon sums up the result: he became greater than anyone before him in Jerusalem. He adds that “my wisdom remained with me,” so he stayed a careful observer throughout his pursuit of pleasure and achievement, and his verdict is a wise man’s judgment, not the regret of someone lost in excess.
9.explain:
So I became great and excelled more than all who were before me in Jerusalem brings the inventory to its result. The word “So” gathers up everything listed in verses 4–8. The man who set out to make his works “great” (verse 4) now says that he himself “became great.” His achievements raised him above everyone who had lived in Jerusalem before him, completing the comparison he began with his herds and flocks in verse 7.

Also my wisdom remained with me explains how Solomon could judge his own experiment. Wisdom, the skill for living and judging well, stayed with him while he pursued pleasure and achievement. This matches verse 3, where he tested wine “while guiding my heart with wisdom.” He was fully immersed in the pursuit and still kept the clear sight to evaluate it. So when he gives his verdict in verse 11, he speaks as someone who saw the experiment clearly from the inside.
9.notes: This verse restates Solomon’s claim in 1:16, where he said, “I have attained greatness, and have gained more wisdom than all who were before me in Jerusalem.” The same three elements return here: greatness, wisdom, and comparison with all who were before him in Jerusalem. In 1:16 the claim belongs to his search into wisdom. Here it concludes his search through pleasure and achievement.

10.brief: Solomon held nothing back: “Whatever my eyes desired I did not keep from them.” He also admits that his work brought him real enjoyment, “my heart rejoiced in all my labor,” and he calls that enjoyment his reward. The verdict that follows therefore does not deny the pleasure he felt. It asks whether that passing pleasure was all his labor could give.
10.explain:
Whatever my eyes desired I did not keep from them shows that the experiment held nothing back. The eyes stand for desire awakened by what a person sees. Earlier Solomon observed that “The eye is not satisfied with seeing” (1:8). Here he gives his eyes everything they want, to learn whether a full supply could finally satisfy them.

I did not withhold my heart from any pleasure carries the same freedom inward. Here “heart” means the inner person, the seat of desire and choice. Solomon gave himself fully to the pursuit, so his experiment cannot be dismissed as a test that never went far enough.

For my heart rejoiced in all my labor makes an honest admission. Solomon genuinely enjoyed his work. The building, planting, and gathering delighted him while he was doing them. This matters for the whole chapter, because his coming verdict does not claim that achievement gave him no pleasure.

And this was my reward from all my labor identifies that enjoyment as what his labor paid him. The reward was real, but the sentence also sets its limits: the enjoyment he felt along the way was what all that labor produced. Verse 11 then asks whether anything more lasting remained once that enjoyment had been received.
10.notes: In the NKJV, “For” and “And” begin with capital letters in the middle of this verse because the translation sets these clauses as separate poetic lines. Verse 11 is laid out the same way.

11.brief: When Solomon looks back over “all the works that my hands had done,” he concludes that “all was vanity and grasping for the wind,” as meaningless as trying to hold the wind in your hand. “There was no profit under the sun”: measured within the limits of earthly life, his great undertaking left no lasting gain beyond the enjoyment he had already received along the way.
11.explain:
Then I looked on all the works that my hands had done marks the moment of assessment. After all the building, planting, and gathering, Solomon steps back to survey the whole. “The works” recalls “I made my works great” in verse 4, and “my hands” stresses that this was his own effort, the achievement of a life spent making things for himself.

And on the labor in which I had toiled widens the review to include the effort itself. Solomon weighs both the results and the work that produced them, including the very labor he admits he enjoyed in verse 10.

And indeed all was vanity and grasping for the wind gives the verdict. “Vanity” translates a Hebrew word whose basic image is breath or vapor, and Solomon uses it to call his whole undertaking meaningless, empty of lasting substance and gone like a breath. “Grasping for the wind” pictures a man closing his hand on moving air and finding it empty. The word “all” leaves nothing out: houses, vineyards, gardens, pools, servants, herds, treasure, and singers fall under the same judgment.

There was no profit under the sun answers the question that opened the book (1:3). Profit is the lasting gain left over after all of one’s labor, and Solomon finds none. “Under the sun” marks the limits of his examination. He measures life by what people can observe and achieve before the grave, and he leaves God’s revelation and future judgment out of the calculation. Within those limits, his great undertaking left nothing beyond the enjoyment he had already received along the way.

This verdict is not the chapter’s last word. God is not named in this chapter until verse 24, where Solomon recognizes that the enjoyment of food, drink, and labor comes “from the hand of God.” The wider witness of Scripture carries the answer further. Because Christ has risen, labor is “not in vain in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 15:58). Work done in Him is not erased by death, the very loss Solomon could not get past under the sun.
11.notes:
The vocabulary of the book’s opening question returns here almost word for word. In 1:3 Solomon asked, “What profit has a man from all his labor In which he toils under the sun?” Verse 11 repeats “labor,” “profit,” and “under the sun,” and its “toiled” matches “toils.”

“Grasping for the wind” appears in nine verses of Ecclesiastes, all between 1:14 and 6:9 (1:14, 17; 2:11, 17, 26; 4:4, 6, 16; 6:9). Within this chapter it returns in verses 17 and 26, linking the verdict on great works with the later verdicts on life and on the sinner’s gathering.

The NLT renders the final sentence “There was nothing really worthwhile anywhere.” That keeps the verdict but does not reproduce “profit” or “under the sun,” and the NLT does not use “profit” in 1:3 either. As a result, the link between this verse and the book’s opening question is less visible in the NLT than in the NKJV.

12.brief: Solomon now sets “wisdom and madness and folly” side by side to weigh them. He asks, “what can the man do who succeeds the king?” and answers, “Only what he has already done.” The question suggests that no one coming after Solomon could take the experiment further than he had, and it also introduces the successor who will trouble him in verses 18–19.
12.explain:
Then I turned myself to consider wisdom and madness and folly — Solomon has just looked over his great works and found “no profit under the sun” (verse 11). Now he takes up a different question: what is wisdom itself worth when it is set beside its opposites? Madness and folly are not new subjects for him. He called laughter “Madness!” in verse 2, and in verse 3 he deliberately set out “to lay hold on folly” while still “guiding my heart with wisdom.” Having lived on both sides of that line, he is in a position to weigh one against the other.

For what can the man do who succeeds the king? — The question explains why Solomon’s assessment carries weight. He is the king who had every resource and denied himself nothing (verses 4–10). Whoever comes after him will work with the same kinds of materials and face the same limits, so Solomon asks what such a person could possibly add.

Only what he has already done — The answer closes the question. A successor can only repeat what has already been tried, so no one will be better placed than Solomon to reach a verdict, and no later king will find a gain that he missed. The words also bring a new figure into view. “The man who will come after me” returns in verses 18–19, where Solomon grieves that he must leave everything he built to him. The passage does not tell us who that successor is.
12.notes:
The three terms in this verse repeat the wording of Ecclesiastes 1:17, “I set my heart to know wisdom and to know madness and folly.” After the tests of pleasure (2:1–3) and great works (2:4–11), Solomon picks up the comparison he began in chapter 1 and carries it through to its conclusion.

The NKJV and NLT understand the second half of the verse differently. The NKJV asks what the king’s successor can do and answers that he can only repeat what has been done. The NLT reads it as Solomon’s own claim to be the best person for the comparison: “for who can do this better than I, the king?” Both renderings arrive at the same point, that no one is better qualified than Solomon to judge. Only the NKJV wording, however, introduces the successor who reappears in verses 18–19.

13.brief: Solomon affirms that wisdom has a real advantage: it is better than folly as surely as light is better than darkness. What follows does not cancel this statement. Wisdom really does help a person see clearly and live well.
13.explain:
Then I saw that wisdom excels folly As light excels darkness — Before Solomon describes the limit of wisdom, he states its value without hedging. “Then I saw” presents the statement as a conclusion he reached through his own testing. To make the comparison he chooses light and darkness, two things no one would treat as equal options. Anyone who has tried to cross a room at night knows how much better it is to have light. Wisdom has that kind of advantage over folly, because it lets a person see what is in front of him, judge situations accurately, and choose a good path.

Solomon never takes this statement back. In the verses that follow he will find that wisdom cannot stop death, but its advantage still holds for the whole of life. Ecclesiastes treats wisdom as skill for living. What the book exposes is the hope that wisdom could be enough on its own to secure a lasting gain.
13.notes: The NLT opens verse 13 with “I thought,” and its quotation runs into verse 14, closing after “fools walk in the dark.” It presents verses 13 and 14a as one thought Solomon voiced to himself. The NKJV uses no quotation marks here, but it also keeps the two statements together as one observation before “Yet” turns the argument in the second half of verse 14.

14.brief: The wise person sees where he is going, while the fool stumbles in darkness, which illustrates the advantage Solomon has just affirmed. Yet he sees that “the same event happens to them all”: death comes to the wise and the fool alike, and wisdom cannot stop it.
14.explain:
The wise man’s eyes are in his head — A person’s eyes sit at the front of the head, where they can look ahead and guide each step. The saying pictures the wise man actually using that sight. He watches where the road leads and notices trouble before he walks into it. In this way the saying illustrates the light Solomon spoke of in verse 13.

But the fool walks in darkness — The fool also has eyes, but he goes through life as though it were night. The darkness of verse 13 has become the place where he lives, so he stumbles into the trouble that wisdom would have seen coming. These two lines describe a difference that shows itself in ordinary decisions every day.

Yet I myself perceived That the same event happens to them all — “Yet” turns the argument. Solomon does not withdraw the contrast he has just drawn. He places beside it something he has seen for himself: one end awaits the wise and the fool. Verses 15–16 make clear that this end is death (“how does a wise man die? As the fool!”). Wisdom can light a person’s path through life, but it has no power to change where every path ends. Sharing that end does not make the wise and the fool the same kind of people. It does show that wisdom’s real advantage cannot carry anyone past the grave.
14.notes:
Ecclesiastes returns to this expression later and makes its meaning plain. In 9:2, “One event happens to the righteous and the wicked,” and 9:3 adds that “one thing happens to all” and that afterward “they go to the dead.” In 3:19 the same idea extends to animals: “one thing befalls them: as one dies, so dies the other.” These passages confirm that “the same event” in 2:14 refers to death.

The NLT renders the phrase as “share the same fate” and then begins verse 15 with “Both will die.” It states outright at the start of verse 15 what the NKJV does not make explicit until the closing question of verse 16.

15.brief: Solomon applies this truth to himself. If he will meet the same end as the fool, he asks, “why was I then more wise?” He concludes, “This also is vanity,” because his wisdom is real but cannot secure the lasting advantage he had hoped it would give him.
15.explain:
So I said in my heart — Solomon now turns his general observation on himself. The words introduce his private reasoning, just as “I said in my heart” opened the test of pleasure in verse 1. What follows is a man thinking honestly about his own death, not a lecture about other people.

As it happens to the fool, It also happens to me — The king who “gained more wisdom than all who were before me in Jerusalem” (1:16) admits that he will meet the fool’s end. His wisdom, however great, will not exempt him from death.

And why was I then more wise? — Here “then” carries the sense of “in that case.” If the wise and the fool end in the same place, Solomon wants to know what all his extra wisdom has gained him. He measures wisdom by the standard he has used throughout his search: what remains for a person when everything is finished. By that measure, the effort of becoming wise seems to have bought nothing lasting.

This also is vanity — Solomon gives his verdict: when wisdom is judged by what it can secure against death, it too proves meaningless. The word “also” joins wisdom to pleasure (verse 1) and to his great works (verse 11), which have already received the same verdict. Wisdom is still better than folly (verse 13). The hope that proves empty is the hope that wisdom could give him a gain that would outlast him.
15.notes: The expression “I said in my heart” appears twice in this verse. It also opens the test of pleasure in 2:1 and returns in 3:17 and 3:18, and 1:16 uses the related wording “I communed with my heart.” Again and again Solomon reports his conclusions as words spoken inwardly, so the reader hears his reasoning as he worked it out.

16.brief: Death is followed by forgetting. The wise are no more remembered than the fool, since “all that now is will be forgotten in the days to come,” and Solomon’s pained question, “And how does a wise man die? As the fool!”, shows that from an earthly point of view even wisdom’s legacy fades. The verse describes the death and forgetting that both share. It does not say that the wise and the fool are equal in character or in their standing before God.
16.explain:
For there is no more remembrance of the wise than of the fool forever — “For” gives the reason behind the verdict of verse 15. Death is not the only thing the wise and the fool share, because both are also forgotten. A wise man might hope that his counsel, his name, or his achievements would keep his memory alive after he is gone. Solomon says that the memory of the wise lasts no longer than the memory of the fool.

Since all that now is will be forgotten in the days to come — The forgetting reaches beyond individual people to everything in the present. The book’s opening poem said the same about every generation: “There is no remembrance of former things” (1:11). Even a famous king’s wisdom will fade as later generations come and go.

And how does a wise man die? As the fool! — Solomon’s grief comes through in the question and its blunt answer. Death comes to the wise exactly as it comes to the fool, and understanding earns no exemption. Within the earthly limits of his search, where life is measured by what lasts before the grave, this is a bitter discovery. Solomon is describing a shared end and a shared forgetting. He is not saying that God sees no difference between wisdom and folly, and the book later declares that “God will bring every work into judgment” (12:14).
16.notes: In the NKJV, the verse closes with a question and an exclamation, which gives its last line the force of a lament. The NLT moves the fact of death to the front (“For the wise and the foolish both die.”) and expresses the whole verse as plain statements, so it conveys the same facts without the closing question.

17.brief: Because the wise and the fool share the same death and are both forgotten, Solomon says, “Therefore I hated life.” The work done “under the sun” distressed him, because when it is measured only by earthly results, all of it seems meaningless and impossible to hold. The verse honestly records the lowest point of his search, but it is not the book’s final counsel.
17.explain:
Therefore I hated life because the work that was done under the sun was distressing to me — “Therefore” ties Solomon’s feeling directly to what he has just observed: the wise and the fool die alike and are forgotten alike. The reason he gives for hating life is that the work done in the world distressed him. “Under the sun” marks the limits of his examination. He is weighing human activity by what can be seen and achieved before the grave, with God’s revelation and judgment left out of the calculation. Measured that way, the work of life brings him only distress.

for all is vanity and grasping for the wind — Solomon repeats the verdict he reached about his great works in verse 11 and now applies it to everything. “Vanity” means that the work is meaningless as a source of lasting gain. “Grasping for the wind” pictures someone reaching for what cannot be held. If death and forgetting erase whatever a person achieves, every effort ends with an empty hand.

Solomon’s words mark the lowest point of his search. Scripture lets that grief be spoken honestly, but it is not the book’s last word. Later in this same chapter Solomon recognizes that eating, drinking, and enjoying good in one’s labor come “from the hand of God” (verse 24). The book closes with the call to fear God and keep His commandments, because He will bring every work into judgment (12:13–14). Ecclesiastes 2 does not name Christ. Read alongside 1 Corinthians 15, however, the problem of death and forgotten work finds its answer in Him: because Christ has risen as the firstfruits, labor in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:20–26, 58).
17.notes:
Verse 17 is the first of two statements of hatred in the chapter. Here Solomon hates life because of the shared death and forgetting described in verses 14–16. In verse 18 he says, “Then I hated all my labor,” because he must leave it to the one who comes after him. Because the two statements mark separate steps in his grief, verse 17 closes this section and verse 18 opens the next.

Within chapter 2, “grasping for the wind” appears in verses 11, 17, and 26. Each time it attaches to a verdict: first on Solomon’s great works, then on all the work done under the sun, and finally on the sinner’s gathering for someone else.

18.brief: Solomon’s grief turns from life in general to his own work: “Then I hated all my labor.” He must leave everything he built to “the man who will come after me,” so death does more than end the worker. It also hands his achievements to someone else.
18.explain:
Then I hated all my labor — In verse 17 Solomon said, “Therefore I hated life.” Now his grief narrows to his own work. The word “Then” links the two statements: the death that the wise and the fool share has already made life seem empty, and the same reality now turns him against everything he has built. The labor he hates here is the result of his work, the houses, vineyards, gardens, and treasures he listed in verses 4–8. The rest of the verse makes this clear, because labor in that sense is something he must hand over to someone else.

in which I had toiled under the sun — This phrase adds the effort behind those achievements. Solomon is not looking at an inheritance he received. He is looking at what cost him years of his own strength and thought. “Under the sun” marks the measure he is using: life judged within earthly limits, by what can be seen and kept before the grave, with God and His future judgment left out of the calculation. Within that horizon, the more a man invests, the more he stands to lose.

because I must leave it to the man who will come after me — Here is the reason for his hatred. Death ends the worker’s life, and it also forces him to give up everything his work produced. Solomon first raised the successor in verse 12 when he asked, “For what can the man do who succeeds the king?” Now that successor becomes the center of his grief. The verse does not name him. Solomon’s distress rests on the plain certainty that someone else will hold what he labored to build.
18.notes:
The NKJV keeps “the man who will come after me” singular, which fits a king thinking about the one who will take his throne and estate. The NLT widens the wording to “leave to others everything I have earned” in this verse and speaks of “my successors” in verse 19. Both renderings describe the same problem. The NKJV keeps the focus on a single heir, and Solomon himself broadens the case to workers in general in verse 21.

The phrase “under the sun” appears in four of the six verses in this section (verses 18, 19, 20, and 22). Its concentration here keeps the earthly measure of Solomon’s reasoning in view as his grief over his labor deepens.

19.brief: No one knows whether this successor “will be wise or a fool,” yet he will rule over everything Solomon worked for and built with wisdom. The worker cannot control what becomes of his work, and Solomon calls this, too, “vanity.”
19.explain:
And who knows whether he will be wise or a fool? — The question expects the answer that no one knows. Solomon has just affirmed that “wisdom excels folly As light excels darkness” (verse 13), so the contrast between the wise and the foolish is still on his mind. The heir’s character matters a great deal, yet it lies beyond the control of the man who leaves him everything. A lifetime of wise work could pass into foolish hands.

Yet he will rule over all my labor — Whatever the successor turns out to be, his authority is certain. “Rule” describes full control: the heir will decide what happens to the houses, lands, and wealth. Solomon cannot know the man’s character, but he knows the man will have the final say over his work.

in which I toiled and in which I have shown myself wise under the sun — Solomon’s achievements were not careless accumulation. He put both effort and wisdom into them, in keeping with verse 9, where he says, “my wisdom remained with me.” That makes the uncertainty sharper. The wisdom invested in the work offers no guarantee that wisdom will govern its future.

This also is vanity. — The Hebrew word translated “vanity” pictures a breath or vapor, something that cannot be held. Here it means that the worker’s situation is meaningless when measured by earthly gain: what he built so carefully slips out of his grasp at death. Solomon does not call wisdom or work worthless. He finds that neither can secure the lasting control of their results that he had hoped for.
19.notes: The verdict “This also is vanity” occurs in verses 19, 21, and 23, and the same words appeared earlier in verse 15. It closes verses 19 and 23, while in verse 21 Solomon extends it by adding “and a great evil.” The repetition gives the section a steady rhythm, with each new angle on the problem of labor returning to the same judgment.

20.brief: Losing control of his work drives Solomon to despair. He gives up any hope that all his labor “under the sun” could bring him lasting gain.
20.explain:
Therefore I turned my heart — “Therefore” ties this despair to the uncertain heir of verse 19. In Ecclesiastes the heart is the center of thought and resolve. Solomon began his search when he said, “I set my heart to seek and search out by wisdom” (1:13), and he opened the test of pleasure when “I said in my heart” (2:1). The same heart that set out with such determination now turns toward despair.

and despaired of all the labor in which I had toiled under the sun — To despair is to give up hope. Solomon does not say he stopped working. He gave up expecting that his labor could bring him a lasting gain he could keep. Within the earthly limits of his examination, that hope had nowhere to stand once he saw that death would hand everything to another. The verse lets this grief be felt honestly. It is still a step in the search, and verse 24 will show where the chapter goes next.
20.notes: The NLT renders the end of this verse as “all my hard work in this world.” Its use of “in this world” for “under the sun,” like “here on earth” in its rendering of verse 18, shows the phrase being read as a description of life on earth measured within its earthly limits.

21.brief: Solomon widens his own case into a general one: a person may work “with wisdom, knowledge, and skill” and still have to leave what he has gained to “a man who has not labored for it.” He calls this “vanity and a great evil,” a grievous misfortune, because the careful worker loses the fruit of his work to someone who did nothing to earn it.
21.explain:
For there is a man whose labor is with wisdom, knowledge, and skill — “For” introduces the reason behind Solomon’s despair, and he now moves from “I” to “a man.” His own case becomes a pattern anyone can recognize. This worker has done everything right. Wisdom gives him good judgment, knowledge gives him understanding, and skill gives him the practical ability to do the work well. His labor is the opposite of careless or lazy effort.

yet he must leave his heritage to a man who has not labored for it — “Heritage” here means what the worker has built up and will pass on: his estate, the fruit of his life’s work. The word “must” shows he has no choice, because death compels the transfer. The one who receives it “has not labored for it.” The verse does not call the heir wicked. It simply sets the careful worker beside someone who enjoys the result without sharing the effort.

This also is vanity and a great evil. — Solomon adds a stronger word to his usual verdict. “Evil” here does not describe a sin committed by the worker or the heir. It describes a calamity, a grievous misfortune in the way things turn out. The careful worker loses what he built to someone who did nothing to earn it, and within the earthly measure Solomon is using, nothing makes that loss right.
21.notes:
Ecclesiastes uses “evil” for misfortune in a closely similar case. In 6:2 Solomon describes a man whose wealth goes to someone else, “but a foreigner consumes it,” and he concludes, “This is vanity, and it is an evil affliction.” The lonely worker of 4:8 receives a parallel verdict: “This also is vanity and a grave misfortune.” These passages confirm that the “great evil” of verse 21 is a painful misfortune rather than moral wickedness.

The NLT translates the closing words as “a great tragedy,” which matches this sense of the verse.

22.brief: Solomon asks again the question that opened the book (1:3), now in personal terms: what does a person finally have to show for all his labor and “the striving of his heart”? When life is measured only by earthly gain, the question expects the answer that nothing lasting remains.
22.explain:
For what has man for all his labor — Solomon returns to the question that opened the book: “What profit has a man from all his labor In which he toils under the sun?” (1:3). After the whole search of 1:12–2:21, he asks it again, now with his own grief behind it. The question is rhetorical. Measured by what a person can keep, the expected answer is that nothing lasting remains.

and for the striving of his heart — Labor involves more than physical work. This phrase adds the inner exertion behind it: the ambition, planning, worry, and drive to succeed. Solomon is asking what all that mental and emotional effort finally yields.

with which he has toiled under the sun? — The closing phrase sets the question within the earthly horizon once more, and inside those limits it has no satisfying answer. The book’s own answer begins two verses later, where enjoyment is received “from the hand of God” (verse 24). The wider witness of Scripture adds more. Because Christ has risen, Paul assures believers that their labor in the Lord is not in vain (1 Corinthians 15:58). Work done in Him is neither erased by death nor lost to an unknown heir.
22.notes: Verse 22 asks “what has man” rather than using the word “profit,” as 1:3 does. Verse 11 had already answered the question with “There was no profit under the sun,” and it returns once more in 3:9: “What profit has the worker from that in which he labors?”

23.brief: Solomon describes what such labor is like day to day: days full of sorrow, work that is a burden, and a heart that “takes no rest” even at night. Work pursued for a lasting gain it cannot give brings restless anxiety, and he calls this also “vanity.”
23.explain:
For all his days are sorrowful — “For” explains why the worker has nothing to show. The trouble does not wait until the end of life, when everything passes to another. The days along the way are full of sorrow as well, and “all his days” covers the whole span of such a life.

and his work burdensome — The work itself becomes a weight. Solomon has in view labor driven by the hope of a lasting gain it cannot give. Such work is heavy because so much is being asked of it.

even in the night his heart takes no rest — The pressure follows the worker to bed. When his body should be resting, his mind keeps turning over plans and worries. Solomon describes an anxiety that never lets go, and many hardworking people know it well.

This also is vanity. — The section ends with the same verdict. Restless toil cannot secure what it strives for, so it too is meaningless when measured by earthly gain. This verse marks the low point of the section, but it is not the chapter’s last word. In the very next verse Solomon turns to food, drink, and enjoyment in labor received as God’s gift.
23.notes:
The word “burdensome” recalls 1:13, where Solomon called his search “this burdensome task God has given to the sons of man.” The search that began as a heavy task reaches the end of this section with work described in the same terms.

Ecclesiastes later says, “The sleep of a laboring man is sweet,” and adds, “But the abundance of the rich will not permit him to sleep” (5:12). Read with verse 23, that saying shows that sleeplessness does not come from work itself. It belongs to the anxious striving and accumulation Solomon describes here.

24.brief: The chapter turns. Nothing is better than to eat, drink, and let one’s soul “enjoy good in his labor,” and Solomon now sees that this enjoyment is “from the hand of God.” He could not produce lasting satisfaction by pursuing pleasure and achievement, but simple enjoyment can be received as God’s gift. This is the first passage in the book that commends joy as His gift.
24.explain:
Nothing is better for a man than that he should eat and drink — After the despair of verses 18–23, Solomon reaches a very different conclusion. Eating and drinking are the most ordinary parts of daily life. Solomon had already tried wine as a way to find what was good (verse 3), and that experiment failed. Here food and drink are no longer a test meant to produce lasting gain. They are simple goods, enjoyed for what they are. Solomon is not saying that nothing else matters. He is saying that, after everything he has tried, nothing open to a person is better than receiving these daily goods.

and that his soul should enjoy good in his labor — The word “soul” places this enjoyment in the person’s inner life, not merely in the body’s appetite. What is surprising is where the enjoyment is found: “in his labor.” Only a few lines earlier Solomon said, “Then I hated all my labor” (verse 18), and he described a worker whose days are sorrowful, whose work is burdensome, and whose heart “takes no rest” even at night (verse 23). The same labor that could not deliver lasting gain can still give real, present good. Solomon had tasted this before, when “my heart rejoiced in all my labor” (verse 10). The difference now lies in where he sees that enjoyment coming from.

This also, I saw, was from the hand of God — “I saw” marks this as something Solomon came to recognize, not something he produced. “The hand of God” pictures God as the giver who places these good things into a person’s life. This is the first time God is named in Ecclesiastes 2. Through verses 1–23 Solomon built, planted, gathered, and weighed everything by what he himself could achieve. When he finally speaks of God, he is not reporting another achievement. He is receiving a gift. Pleasure failed when Solomon tried to make it the foundation of life, yet eating, drinking, and work are not condemned by the verdict of verse 11. Received from God, those same ordinary joys are good.
24.notes:
The wording of verse 24 echoes the end of verse 23 with the opposite result. Verse 23 closes, “This also is vanity,” while verse 24 closes, “This also, I saw, was from the hand of God.” The repeated “This also” sets the meaningless toil of the anxious worker directly beside the enjoyment that comes as God’s gift.

The phrase “under the sun” appears five times in verses 17–22 (verses 17, 18, 19, 20, and 22) but not at all in verses 24–26. Its absence fits the shift from Solomon’s earthbound calculation to his recognition of God’s gift. Later enjoyment passages do use the phrase (5:18; 8:15), so the absence here is worth noticing but is not a rule for the whole book.

Ecclesiastes returns to this conviction later and names it directly as a gift. Solomon says that every man should “eat and drink and enjoy the good of all his labor—it is the gift of God” (3:13), and of the power “to receive his heritage and rejoice in his labor” he says, “this is the gift of God” (5:19). These parallels confirm that “from the hand of God” in verse 24 describes God’s giving.

25.brief: Solomon backs this conclusion with his own experience: no one could eat or enjoy more than he had. Because he had tried every pleasure, his testimony that enjoyment comes from God’s hand carries special weight.
25.explain:
For who can eat — The opening “For” ties this verse to verse 24 and gives a reason to trust Solomon’s conclusion. His question is rhetorical, and the answer he expects is “no one.” Solomon had a king’s resources and had used them without restraint. Earlier in the chapter he said, “Whatever my eyes desired I did not keep from them” (verse 10).

or who can have enjoyment, more than I? — No one had pursued enjoyment more fully than Solomon, and that is why his testimony matters. When the man who tried every pleasure says that simple enjoyment comes from God’s hand, he speaks from experience, not from lack of opportunity. He had learned that abundance could not produce lasting gain, yet he does not now despise eating and enjoyment. He puts them in their proper place, as gifts received from God rather than achievements that could secure meaning.
25.notes: The NLT renders this verse quite differently: “For who can eat or enjoy anything apart from him?” In that rendering the pronoun “him” refers back to God in verse 24, so the question points to God as the source of enjoyment. The NKJV’s “more than I” points instead to Solomon’s own unmatched experience as support for verse 24. The two translations reflect different understandings of the underlying wording, but both connect enjoyment with God’s gift in verse 24: the NKJV through Solomon’s testimony, the NLT through its pronoun “him,” which points back to God.

26.brief: God gives “wisdom and knowledge and joy to a man who is good in His sight,” but to the sinner He gives “the work of gathering and collecting” for the benefit of the one who is good before God. This places enjoyment within a right relationship with God, but it is not a promise that the faithful will grow rich. The closing words, “This also is vanity and grasping for the wind,” describe the futility of the sinner’s gathering, which he never finally keeps. They do not cancel the gift affirmed in verse 24.
26.explain:
For God gives wisdom and knowledge and joy — Once again “For” explains what came before. Enjoyment comes from God’s hand because God is the One who gives. Wisdom and knowledge were the very things Solomon pursued when his search began, and by his own effort they only increased his grief (1:18). Here they stand beside joy as gifts that God gives, not prizes a person can seize.

to a man who is good in His sight — God’s gift is connected with a person’s standing before Him. “In His sight” means as God sees and judges, not as people measure success. This places enjoyment within a right relationship with God. The verse does not explain how someone comes to be good in God’s sight. It shows that God’s gifts are not detached from a person’s relationship with Him.

but to the sinner He gives the work of gathering and collecting — The sinner also receives something from God, but what he receives is a task rather than enjoyment. “The work of gathering and collecting” pictures restless accumulation: piling up goods without ever coming to rest in them. The phrase recalls the worker of verses 22–23, whose labor and “striving of his heart” left him sorrowful by day and sleepless at night.

that he may give to him who is good before God — What the sinner gathers ends up with someone else, the person who is good before God. This speaks to the bitter problem of verses 18–21, where a worker had to leave his labor to “a man who has not labored for it.” Here the transfer of what a person gathers is placed under God’s hand. Verse 26 describes a general pattern in God’s ordering of life. It does not promise that every faithful person will become wealthy or inherit a sinner’s estate. Ecclesiastes itself admits that just people sometimes receive what the wicked deserve (8:14), and it leaves the final settling of every account to God’s judgment: “God will bring every work into judgment” (12:14).

This also is vanity and grasping for the wind — Solomon closes the chapter with a refrain he has used before (verses 11 and 17). Here it most naturally describes the sinner’s gathering. He works to collect and keep, yet what he gathers passes to another, so his effort is meaningless, as empty as trying to hold the wind in your hand. The refrain does not withdraw the gift of verse 24. The enjoyment God gives remains good. What proves empty is the grasping that tries to hold what it can never finally keep.
26.notes:
The pairing of “wisdom and knowledge” repeats the pair Solomon used near the start of his search: “My heart has understood great wisdom and knowledge” (1:16), followed by the discovery that “he who increases knowledge increases sorrow” (1:18). The search that began with wisdom and knowledge as personal attainments ends with them listed among God’s gifts.

The NKJV speaks only of “the work of gathering and collecting.” The NLT gives the clause a financial meaning: “if a sinner becomes wealthy, God takes the wealth away.” The NKJV wording is broader. It describes the activity of accumulating without naming wealth or explaining how the transfer takes place.

In the NKJV, the sinner’s “gathering” uses the same English verb Solomon used for his own accumulation: “I also gathered for myself silver and gold” (verse 8). The verse does not identify Solomon as the sinner. Still, the repeated word sets the restless gathering of verse 26 beside the self-directed acquiring that the chapter has already found empty.

The refrain itself does not say what “This” refers to. On its own it could be heard as a summary of the whole verse or even of the whole search, not only of the sinner’s gathering that immediately precedes it.
